                    ### Question
                    A 25-year-old woman presented to an urgent care center with a complaint of a cough for more than 3 weeks that was accompanied by night sweats, weight loss, and malaise. On physical examination, the patient had slightly pale palpebral conjunctivae bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, but with no adventitious breath sounds in the lung fields bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was routine. The patient was started on a drug regimen that was to be taken for 6 months. On follow-up after 2 months, the ALT and AST levels were elevated. Which of the following anti-tubercular drug could have contributed to this labor result?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rifampicin
opb. Pyrazinamide
opc. Isoniazid
opd. Streptomycin
ope. Ethambutol

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of cough, night sweats, weight loss, and malaise, along with cervical lymphadenopathy, strongly suggest a diagnosis of tuberculosis. The initiation of anti-tubercular treatment led to elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST) after 2 months. Among the options, Pyrazinamide is well-documented to cause hepatotoxicity and is a common contributor to elevated liver enzymes in patients undergoing tuberculosis treatment. Isoniazid can also cause liver enzyme elevation, but it is less frequently the primary cause compared to Pyrazinamide. Rifampicin, Streptomycin, and Ethambutol are generally not associated with significant liver toxicity. Therefore, the most likely drug contributing to the elevated liver enzymes is Pyrazinamide, supported by its known hepatotoxic effects in clinical practice.
